newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: AUSTRALIANS THANKED FOR ABORIGINAL RECOGNITION
An Aboriginal elder has thanked the 11 and a half million Australians who voted for Aboriginal people's rights in the 1967 referendum.
Ruth Heggarty was addressing a rally in central Brisbane as part of a national day of action commemorating the referendum.
She says the 92 per cent vote to give Aboriginal people full rights as Australian citizens was the high point in Aboriginal affairs.
Ms Heggarty says it was a bit of a joke that the constitution needed to be amended to allow the Aboriginal inhabitants of Australia to be counted in reckoning the population.
But she says they are now recognised as human beings with basic human rights.
GOVT AND ALP AT LOGGERHEADS OVER ABORIGINAL MOTION
The Federal Government looks unlikely to win bi-partisan support for its Parliamentary motion to mark the 30th anniversary of the 1967 referendum which granted Aborigines equal rights.
The Prime Minister intends moving a motion endorsing the referendum and giving an on-going commitment to the reconciliation process.
But Labor wants the motion to include an apology for the past treatment of indigenous people, particularly those forcibly removed from their families as children.
Mr Howard would rather the motion focus on practical ways of helping indigenous Australians, such as improving health, education and housing services.
GOVERNMENT ACCUSED OF BANK BASHING
The Australian Bankers Association says the Federal Government has gone over the top with bank bashing.
The Prime Minister and the Treasurer have criticised the big four banks for not passing on the full half per cent cut in official interest rates last Friday.
Treasurer, Peter Costello yesterday recommended borrowers go to mortgage-originators for their home loans rather than banks.
Association Executive Director, Mark Addis, says the comments were quite extraordinary.
Mr Addis says the banking industry encourages customers to shop around on price and product, and the Government shouldn't dictate where customers should shop.
He says the Government's comments smack of glib political point-scoring.
GOVT CRITICISED FOR BACKFLIP ON VETERANS
Federal Opposition Leader, Kim Beazley, says it's regrettable that the Government's decided to go back on its pre-election promise to award medals to veterans of the so-called forgotten wars.
The Coalition had pledged to decorate people who fought in conflicts like the Korean War and the Malay emergency, but Cabinet now says such a presentation would be superfluous.
The Government says these servicemen and women have already received imperial awards for their services.
Mr Beazley says the veterans have every right to feel betrayed.
He says it's not a difficult or expensive move for the Government to make, and yet they've decided not to pursue it.
PARALYSED ABALONE DIVER SET FOR HUGE PAY-OUT
A man from the New South Wales south coast is expected to receive at least eight-million-dollars compensation after a car accident ended his abalone diving career.
The New South Wales Supreme Court has today calculated the damages pay-out to Clyde Thomas, who was left a quadraplegic in a road accident at Bega in 1989.
Justice Carolyn Simpson described the 44-year-old man from Eden as an energetic, motivated and determined diver before the crash.

While the exact size of the pay-out has yet to be finalised, the Court has assessed the damages eight-million-dollars, including two-million-dollars for future care and almost three-million-dollars for lost income.
CIRCUSES WITH EXOTIC ANIMALS BANNED
Liverpool Council in Sydney has joined a growing number of local government bodies banning circuses featuring exotic animals.
Liverpool voted last night to outlaw circuses that have animals like elephants or lions, as well as any native wild animals.
Councillor Allison McGarrity says public opinion does not support wild animals being kept by travelling circuses.
She says Liverpool has joined 10 other councils in the Sydney area in banning the acts.
ONE DOSE CHILDREN'S HEP-A VACCINE AVAILABLE
A one-dose vaccine to protect children from Hepatitis-A becomes available today.
The vaccine, for children aged from two to 15 years, gives one year of protection, with a booster dose after six-months extending cover for as long as 25 years.
Hepatitis-A is the most common vaccine preventable disease which affects travellers - particularly to the poorer or developing regions of the world.
The Director of the Travellers' Medical and Vaccination Centre, John Cottrell-Dormer, says it may also be useful in preventing the spread of the disease.
BIG INDUSTRY SUPER FUND OPENING TO PUBLIC
One of Australia's biggest industry superannuation funds is to become open to public membership.
The Superannuation Trust of Australia, which is jointly managed by the Metal Trades Industry Association and unions, has mainly serviced the manufacturing sector.
But STA Chairman, Bert Evans, says any employee or self employed person will now be able to join the fund.
The move follows the release of the Wallis Report which reccomends industry funds be opened up to competition, with employees able to choose which scheme they join.
